title: A2UI 1.0 stabilizes generated interfaces, with a mixed-version ecosystem
summary: A2UI 1.0 adds a stable protocol, bidirectional calls and stronger composition rules. Express remains a compact generation format, while renderer versions, SDK behavior and application permissions still need separate checks.

sections.title: The November release changes the adoption decision
sections.html:
Google's November 11 announcement makes A2UI 1.0 the first stable release of its generative-interface protocol. It adds bidirectional function calls, accessibility support and extension metadata. The underlying idea remains the one covered here in October: an agent describes an interface, and the host renders it using registered components. This report retains its original identity and October 27 publication date while updating the adoption guidance for the new release.

Stability does not mean every host already accepts 1.0. Google identifies Jetpack Compose and Gemini Enterprise as supporting 0.9.1, with upgrades ahead; Lynx supports 0.9 and is adapting. The announcement lists web, Flutter and SwiftUI rendering routes and examples in Jira, Alation and Gemini Notebook. Those examples show documented adoption, not independent verification that any proposed application will work across all those surfaces.

For a team already evaluating Express, the useful change is a clearer protocol target and migration path. Choose the renderer that users actually need, then negotiate a compatible protocol and catalog. Preserve a working fallback while moving through the transition. A stable standard can reduce uncertainty about the interface contract, but the application still owns its data, actions and user experience. No SDK or demo was installed or executed for this update.

sections.title: Keep model output, transport and trusted data separate
sections.html:
The current inference-format documentation separates the notation a model writes from the JSON messages delivered to a renderer. Express uses compact component constructors and data assignments; deterministic code compiles them into wire messages. Direct JSON and custom formats can target the same renderer. Changing the generation format is therefore different from changing the protocol version or the host's component implementation.

The macro guide describes server-side functions that expand a compact request into existing catalog components. Macros currently belong to the Python agent SDK. A model can name a record while trusted code looks it up and supplies the displayed values. Expansion can change on the server without requiring a new client component, provided the resulting components are already supported. The guide also calls for session-scoped macro state.

Consider a workshop-booking card. The model can choose a session identifier and arrange an explanation, while application code supplies its actual time, capacity and price. Missing records, unauthorized access and capacity changes still need explicit handling. A valid component tree can display a false statement or invite an impermissible action. Inspect syntax, source data and authorization as separate checks, and make the final confirmation refer to the current record rather than an earlier generated summary.

sections.title: Migrate the contract and verify the installed packages
sections.html:
The SDK guide now organizes implementation into Core, Agent and Renderer layers. Its tables list TypeScript and Dart agent support for 0.9.1 and 1.0, Python support including older 0.8, and renderer support that varies by framework. React, Angular, Lit, Flutter and SwiftUI list 1.0; Jetpack Compose lists 0.9.1. These are documented compatibility claims. This research did not check every package-registry release or demonstrate that a locally installed version implements all current documentation.

The evolution guide describes substantive migration work: the 1.0 envelope, explicit catalog protocol metadata, initial components and data in createSurface, and reserved @-prefixed binding and component-envelope keys. It warns against blanket replacement of ordinary path or call properties. Mixed catalogs within a surface must use the same specification version. Treat the guide as a migration specification, not a search-and-replace recipe.

The October 28 inspection found a default switch under Unreleased and complete-reply Express compilation in the launch description. Those remain dated historical observations. Current documentation instead describes Express as the default in the Agent SDK and incremental compilation and validation of streamed output. That is a material documentary update, not a retrospective correction of what the older sources said. Test the exact package, catalog, protocol and renderer combination before relying on progressive rendering.

A focused migration fixture should include a data binding, a normal dictionary containing a path field, an invalid parent-child relationship and an interrupted stream. Preserve expected messages and visible behavior. Verify that an unsupported version produces a recoverable error, and that updating a neighboring component does not discard entered text or keyboard focus. The protocol's new rules provide testable obligations; passing them still requires an actual implementation check.

sections.title: Read each benchmark with its date and denominator
sections.html:
The October 27 announcement described 51 tasks on gemini-3.5-flash and reported up to threefold reductions in generated tokens and latency. The current inference-format page describes a different 54-sample core_v1_0 suite using gemini-3.8-flash at temperature 0.0. Both formats achieve 53 of 54 Pass@1 results in the shown comparison. With unbounded thinking, median code tokens fall from 794 to 260, while total output including thinking falls from 2,320 to 1,789. These are publisher measurements, not an Observatory reproduction.

The distinction changes the interpretation. Roughly three times less generated interface code does not imply three times less total billed output or three times faster completion. Thinking, retries, transport and rendering can dominate the experience. The older and newer suites should not be combined into a trend without matching tasks and settings. A local comparison should count all requests needed to reach an acceptable screen.

The earlier Apparite, or jev2ui, experiment remains a separate architectural example. Its inspected README reported one 11-prompt run with jev-1.13.0, gemini-3.5-flash-lite and a paid Gemini key, with first-component timings distinct from completed-screen timings. It called the results preliminary and the interface a mock. Those historical observations do not establish the current application's performance or working business actions. The November release still places official decision-model SDK support on the roadmap; an experimental Jev integration should not be presented as a shipped universal option.

sections.title: A teacher-facing resource chooser
sections.html:
A useful educational pilot would be a teacher’s resource-selection panel, not an unconstrained student tutor. Define a small catalog containing a resource card, subject filter, duration selector, source link and confirmation control. Give the generator a clear task: help the teacher compare already approved resources for a lesson. Keep curriculum data and resource availability in ordinary application storage. The generated interface can arrange and explain those records while the teacher makes the selection.

Begin with examples that have known answers: an empty collection, several similar resources, a long title, a missing description and a resource unavailable in the requested language. Compare Express with the existing presentation using the same content. Measure whether teachers find the intended resource and understand why it appears. A visually convincing interface that silently drops a prerequisite has failed even if compilation succeeds. This is a proposed evaluation workflow, not evidence of classroom deployment or improved learning outcomes.

Include keyboard navigation, focus behavior, readable labels and a static list alternative in the acceptance criteria. Test whether errors leave the teacher with a recoverable choice instead of a blank panel. The launch does not establish accessibility for every generated composition, and no live interface was tested for this report. Because the host owns the components, the team has a concrete place to implement those requirements; it must still verify the combinations that generation produces.

Also test a change made while a response is arriving. A teacher might select a language and then revise it before the next resource card appears. The application should preserve the newer choice and make any stale recommendation obvious. Save the selected resource identifiers and teacher edits so the lesson can be reproduced later, even if a subsequent model response arranges the cards differently. Review whether a screen reader announces changes usefully without reading every small update. These acceptance criteria connect the protocol's state and accessibility features to a concrete classroom preparation task.

sections.title: Choose expressive generation only where it earns its place
sections.html:
For an app or website, begin with a screen whose decision is easy to describe, such as comparing appointment slots or reviewing a change before submission. Keep the catalog small. Define which values come from trusted records and which text the model may draft. Give users a visible way to revise a selection and inspect its underlying information. Permissions and state transitions remain enforced by application code.

A known settings page may suit controlled selection among developer-authored layouts. Code can determine required fields and ordering while a decision model chooses a relevant pattern. A2UI can carry the resulting messages, but the November announcement still describes official SDK support for models such as Jev as future work. Adopting that pattern today requires a verified integration rather than assuming a documented toggle exists.

For more open-ended screens, compare Express with a fixed template using the same content and task. Record malformed output, repairs, unusable screens and user corrections alongside time to first interaction and completion. A generated arrangement should help users find the information they need without surprising them on every visit. Require a stable fallback when the model or compiler fails. This is a proposed pilot, not evidence that generation improves every form or dashboard.

sections.title: A review interface around a video workflow
sections.html:
A video team could use the same architecture for a transcript-review panel. The host would supply verified timecodes and clip identifiers, while generated cards organize candidate passages by topic or review status. Selecting a card could open the corresponding clip through application code. A producer might compare two alternative outlines without asking the model to construct an entire editing application. This is a proposed surrounding workflow; Express does not itself generate video, understand footage or export an editable timeline.

Separate source facts from editorial suggestions. A timecode should come from the transcript or media index, while a suggested title can be visibly labeled as a draft. Test clips with repeated phrases, missing transcripts and unusually long captions. The interface should make it possible to return to the original passage and correct the selection. A small saved state may be more useful than an impressive screen that cannot reproduce the producer’s decision later.

Apparite is particularly relevant as a prototype reference, but its README explicitly describes an apparition as a mock with no application data or logic behind it. Its comparison pipelines log button and form events rather than implementing the business action. That distinction matters when showing a prototype to a production team. A convincing review screen is evidence of a design possibility; connecting it to media storage, edit decisions and publishing remains separate engineering work.

sections.title: Access, cost and a bounded adoption decision
sections.html:
The October 28 inspection found Apache-2.0 licenses in the A2UI and Apparite repositories. It also recorded the then-current demo prerequisites: Node 18 or later, uv and a Gemini key for the restaurant example; Node 20 or later and Gemini/Jev keys for Apparite. These are preserved historical observations, not a fresh installation guide. For a new 1.0 pilot, use the current quickstart and pin dependencies after confirming the chosen renderer's supported protocol.

No complete current hosted-model price comparison or local-model hardware requirement was established here. Budget for input, reasoning, output, repair calls, hosting and human review. Controlled generation may add decision calls while reducing text generation, so counting only one model's output misses part of the system. A smaller payload can also produce a poor interface that costs more to correct.

A useful first trial has one catalog, one compatible renderer and a small set of representative tasks. Preserve the generated description, compiled messages and observed user outcome. Classify failures as syntax, data, layout, accessibility or application behavior. Expand only when the actual user task is easier and the benefit survives error handling. A2UI 1.0 provides a stronger shared contract; reliable permissions, usable composition and economical operation still depend on the application that implements it.

Keep the pilot's stopping condition explicit. If a repair loop repeatedly produces the same invalid relationship, stop and show the existing form or list with the user's entered data intact. Record the failing payload for later diagnosis. An interface that recovers predictably from a modest failure is often more valuable than one that occasionally generates an impressive arrangement but leaves users unable to finish.

useCases: Generated app and website review panels
limitations: No SDK installation, live product execution or independent latency benchmark.
Current docs describe1.0 and streaming, but exact installed package/registry combinations were not verified.
Jetpack Compose and Gemini Enterprise remain documented at 0.9.1; Lynx at 0.9 in the November 11 announcement.
October Apparite results and demo prerequisites are dated history, not current runtime tests.
Official decision-model SDK support remains roadmap work; no complete hosted-model cost schedule verified.

judgment: A material protocol milestone supports a focused migration or developer pilot. Choose a compatible renderer, preserve trusted-data and permission boundaries, and measure accepted user outcomes rather than generated-token savings alone.
researchNote: November 14 update uses official 1.0 announcement and protocol, SDK, inference-format and macro documentation saved through public web extraction. The coordinator independently inspected the public announcement in the in-app browser; worker browser unavailable. October 28 source observations retain their original dates. No code or demo execution; proposed education/app/web/video workflows are editorial suggestions.
